I am 69 years old and have been farming these fields in Quzhou for half a century. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. My family has seven mouths, and some of my children and grandchildren work in the factories or in Handan, yet they always come back when the wheat needs harvesting or the cotton needs picking. I have twelve mu in total, and I cannot afford to be lazy or wasteful at my age.

This year, I will keep eight mu in the wheat–maize rotation and four mu in cotton. The wheat–maize system is the backbone of our village; it puts food on the table and straw in the shed. I will plant improved wheat in late autumn after rotary tillage, because a fine seedbed stops the cold wind from hurting the roots. I will irrigate three times from the well—once before winter to help the crop survive the frost, once at jointing, and once at filling—because the sky here never gives enough rain at the right moment. I will spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea; I have learned that about eighteen to twenty jin of nitrogen per mu is enough to get a good stand without burning money. I will spray pesticide twice, mainly for aphids and rust, because if you let them start, they spread like gossip.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will sow hybrid maize immediately. Everyone now uses no-tillage for maize after wheat; there is no time to plough, and the old rotary machine only disturbs the roots. The maize needs two good irrigations—one at knee height and one at tasseling—and two rounds of herbicide and insecticide. Hybrid seed costs more, but it yields over a thousand jin per mu, so the extra money pays for itself.

The four mu of cotton I keep for cash. Cotton is backbreaking—planting, thinning, spraying, and picking all by hand—but the price is steady and my daughters-in-law help with the picking in autumn. I will rotary till the cotton plot in spring, plant an improved variety like the ones from the county station, and irrigate three times. Cotton bollworms are vicious here, so I will spray six times during the season; it is a lot of work, but if you skip even one spray you can lose half the crop. I keep the fertilizer a little lower than the young men do, because at my age I would rather have a safe, certain yield than gamble on the weather.

I know every well and every ridge on these twelve mu, and I know what my body can still do. This plan is not fancy, but it has kept my family fed for fifty years, and it will do so for one more season.
